title: The Industrial Revolution
bigQuestion: How did machines, coal and factories change the way people worked, lived and thought, and who paid the price for that change?

story.title: Twelve Hours in the Spinning Room
story.kicker: In Manchester in 1833, a ten-year-old girl walks to work in the dark, and a government official is waiting to ask her how long she stays.
paragraphs: It is half past five on a winter morning in 1833 in Manchester, England. A girl named Ellen, ten years old, pulls on a shawl and walks with her older brother through streets still black with night. The air smells of coal smoke. Around them hundreds of other people move in the same direction, toward the long brick buildings by the river whose windows are already lit. A bell rings at six. Anyone who arrives after it is fined part of a day's pay. Ellen has been walking this route since she was eight.

Inside, the spinning room is hot and loud. Machines called mules stretch across the floor, each one pulling hundreds of threads at once and rolling back and forth on wheels. Ellen's job is to be small. She crawls under the moving frame to sweep up loose cotton and to tie broken threads, then rolls out before the frame comes back. The overlooker, the man in charge of the room, carries a leather strap. Children who fall asleep or slow down feel it. The mule spinner Ellen works for is paid by how much thread he makes, so he pushes her too.

She works until noon, gets forty minutes for bread and cold tea, and works again until seven or eight in the evening. Twelve hours or more, six days a week. Her wage is a few shillings, which her family needs; her father's job weaving cloth at home has disappeared, because the mill's power looms make cloth cheaper than he can. By the end of the day her ankles hurt and her ears ring. Doctors will later describe children like her: knees bent from standing, chests weak from cotton dust, growth stunted.

This year is different for one reason. Parliament has sent inspectors to ask factory children how long they work and what happens to them. Their reports, and the testimony of children and parents before a committee the year before, shock readers who have never been inside a mill. In 1833 Parliament passes a Factory Act. Children under nine may not work in textile mills. Children nine to thirteen may work no more than nine hours a day and must have some schooling. Four inspectors are hired to enforce the law across the whole country. It is a small start, but it is the first time the government has said that what happens to Ellen is its business.

Ellen is not a real person, but everything about her day comes from the records: the hours, the strap, the dust, the ruined home weaver, the inspectors' questions. The Industrial Revolution made Britain the richest country on earth. It also made childhoods like hers, and it made people argue about what a rich country owed the people who produced its wealth. That argument, about work, machines, cities and fairness, is the subject of this chapter.
story.think: Ellen's family needed her wages, and her father's old job was gone. If you could pass one law in 1833, what would it be, and who might be hurt by it?

lessons.title: Coal, Capital and Canals
lessons.mainIdea: Britain industrialized first because it had cheap coal, money to invest, waterways to move heavy goods, and laws that made business relatively safe.
reading: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain, an island with a smaller population than France, rather than somewhere else? Historians point to a set of advantages that came together around 1750. The first was *coal*. Britain had large coalfields close to the surface and near rivers and the sea. Wood was running out as forests were cleared, and coal burned hotter. Cheap coal meant cheap heat for iron furnaces, and later cheap power for steam engines. A country that had to burn wood or import fuel could not have run thousands of factories.

The second advantage was money. Britain had grown rich from trade across the Atlantic, including the trade in enslaved people and the sugar and tobacco they produced. Merchants, landowners and bankers had *capital*, money saved up and available to invest. Britain had a national bank, a stock market and a system of country banks that could lend a mill owner money to build. Interest rates were low. Someone with a good idea and a friend at the bank could try it.

The third was transport. Coal and iron are heavy, and a horse on a muddy road can pull only so much. In 1761 the Duke of Bridgewater opened a canal that carried coal from his mines into Manchester and cut the price of coal in the city by about half. Others copied him. Within fifty years Britain had a network of canals linking mines, factories, rivers and ports. A single horse walking a towpath could pull a barge carrying many tons. Later, railroads would do the same job faster.

Finally, Britain's laws helped. Parliament, not the king, controlled taxes, and Parliament was full of landowners and merchants who protected property. Courts enforced contracts. Patents let inventors profit from their ideas for a set number of years. Britain also had a large market with no internal tolls, unlike France or the German states, and colonies that bought its goods. None of these alone caused the revolution. Together they made Britain the place where a new idea could become a business.

words.d: a black rock formed from ancient plants that burns hot; the main fuel of the Industrial Revolution
money or property saved up and used to start or grow a business
a legal right that lets an inventor control who uses an invention for a set number of years

look.title: British Coal Output
look.prompt: By roughly how many times did coal output grow between 1800 and 1900? What would need to be true about mines, transport and demand to make that possible?

check.q: Why was coal so important to the start of industrialization in Britain?
choices: It was cheap, plentiful and close to rivers, giving heat and power when wood was running out
It was the only fuel that could be exported
It was found only in London
It replaced water as the drink of factory workers
check.why: Britain's shallow, well-placed coalfields gave cheap fuel for furnaces and engines as forests were cleared.

check.q: What does capital mean in this lesson?
choices: The main city of a country
A large factory building
Money saved up and available to invest in a business
A tax on imported goods
check.why: Capital is money or property used to start or grow a business; British merchants and banks had a lot of it to lend.

check.q: What effect did the Bridgewater Canal have on Manchester?
choices: It flooded the city
It made the city a port for ocean ships
It ended the use of horses
It cut the price of coal in the city by about half
check.why: The canal let a single horse pull many tons of coal by barge, sharply lowering the cost of fuel in Manchester.

lessons.title: Cotton and the First Machines
lessons.mainIdea: Demand for cotton cloth drove a chain of inventions in spinning and weaving that moved cloth-making from cottages into mills.
reading: Before 1760 most cloth in Britain was made at home. A farm family bought raw wool or cotton, the women and children spun it into thread on a spinning wheel, and the man wove the thread into cloth on a hand loom. A merchant collected the cloth and paid by the piece. This *cottage industry* was slow. One weaver needed the thread of several spinners, and spinners could not keep up. Meanwhile buyers wanted more cotton cloth, which was light, easy to wash and cheaper than linen or wool. Cotton itself came from India, the Caribbean and, increasingly, the slave plantations of the American South.

Inventors attacked the bottleneck. Around 1764 James Hargreaves, a weaver in Lancashire, built the spinning jenny, a hand-powered frame that let one worker spin eight threads at once, and later far more. In 1769 Richard Arkwright patented the water frame, which used a water wheel to drive rollers that spun stronger thread. Because a water frame needed a river and was too big for a cottage, Arkwright built a mill at Cromford in 1771 and brought workers to the machines. Samuel Crompton's spinning mule of 1779 combined both ideas and became the standard machine of the cotton mill.

Now the problem flipped: spinners made more thread than hand weavers could use. In 1785 Edmund Cartwright patented a power loom. It took decades to perfect, but by the 1820s and 1830s power looms were driving hand weavers out of work. A hand-loom weaver who had earned a decent living in 1800 could barely feed a family by 1830. Some weavers, called Luddites, smashed machines in 1811 and 1812. Parliament made machine-breaking a crime punishable by death. Cheap cotton cloth was a triumph for buyers and a disaster for the people the machines replaced.

The numbers show the scale. Britain imported a few million pounds of raw cotton a year in the 1760s and hundreds of millions of pounds by the 1830s. Cotton cloth became Britain's largest export, sold in India, Latin America and Africa. The city of Manchester, where much of it was made, was nicknamed Cottonopolis. And because the raw cotton came mainly from the American South, the mills of Lancashire and the slave plantations of Mississippi were linked in one system. The machines were new; some of the labor behind them was as old as slavery.

words.d: making goods at home by hand, usually for a merchant who pays by the piece
cloth, or the business of making cloth
a worker in the 1810s who broke machines that were taking away jobs; now used for anyone who resists new technology

look.title: The Weaver's Choice
look.text: A hand-loom weaver in 1828 has worked at home for thirty years. His pay per piece has fallen by more than half since 1800 because power looms make the same cloth faster. His two daughters could earn steady wages at the new mill in town, but he would have to move to the city and give up his loom.
look.prompt: What are his options, and what does each one cost him? Why might people in his position have smashed machines fifteen years earlier?

check.q: What was the bottleneck that the spinning jenny solved?
choices: Spinners could not make thread fast enough to supply weavers
Weavers could not find enough customers
Cotton could not be grown in Britain
Mills had no source of power
check.why: Hand spinning was slow, and one weaver used the output of several spinners; the jenny let one person spin many threads at once.

check.q: Why did Arkwright build a mill instead of selling water frames to families?
choices: Families refused to buy them
The water frame needed a river for power and was too big for a cottage
Parliament required all machines to be in mills
He wanted to keep the invention secret
check.why: A water-powered machine had to sit beside a river, so workers came to the machine rather than the machine coming to them.

check.q: How were the cotton mills of Manchester linked to slavery?
choices: Mill workers in Manchester were enslaved
Manchester sold its cloth only to plantations
Most raw cotton for the mills was grown by enslaved people in the American South
The mills were owned by American planters
check.why: British mills depended on raw cotton from slave plantations, tying free wage labor in England to forced labor in America.

lessons.title: Steam Changes Everything
lessons.mainIdea: James Watt's improved steam engine freed factories from rivers and turned coal into motion, powering mills, mines and eventually ships and trains.
reading: Water wheels had a problem: a mill had to sit by a fast river, and in a dry summer or a hard frost the wheel stopped. Early *steam engines*, used since the early 1700s to pump water out of coal mines, were huge, slow and burned enormous amounts of fuel. In the 1760s a Scottish instrument maker named James Watt, repairing one of these pumps at the University of Glasgow, saw why it wasted so much coal. The cylinder was heated and cooled with every stroke. Watt added a separate condenser so the cylinder stayed hot. His engine used about a quarter of the fuel.

Watt had the idea but not the money. He partnered with Matthew Boulton, a Birmingham manufacturer with capital and factory experience. Their engines, sold from 1776, at first pumped mines. Then Watt worked out how to turn the engine's up-and-down motion into a turning wheel, and by the 1780s steam could drive the spinning machines in a cotton mill. Now a mill could be built anywhere coal could be delivered, including in the middle of a city near workers and markets. Manchester, on a slow river, became a steam city.

Steam power was not sudden. In 1800 most British factories still used water, and many stayed with it for decades. But the trend was clear. Each engine did the work of dozens of horses without tiring. Engineers kept improving them; by the 1800s high-pressure engines were small and strong enough to move themselves. In 1825 the first public steam railway opened in the north of England, and in 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway carried passengers and cotton between the port and the mills at speeds no one had ever traveled on land.

The steam engine changed how people thought about power itself. For all of history, work had been done by muscle, wind, water or fire in a hearth. Now heat from buried rock could be turned into motion on demand. The word horsepower, which Watt invented to sell his engines by comparing them to horses, is still on engines today. Steam also tied industry to coal for good. Every mill chimney in Manchester, and the smoke that blackened its sky, was a Watt engine at work.

words.d: a machine that burns fuel to boil water and uses the pressure of steam to move a piston
the separate chamber Watt added to cool steam so the main cylinder could stay hot
a unit of power that Watt defined by comparing an engine to the work of horses

look.title: Where to Build the Mill
look.text: In 1790 a cloth merchant has money to build one mill. Option one is a water-powered mill on a fast river in a hill valley, forty miles from the nearest town, where he must build houses for workers and haul cotton in by cart. Option two is a steam mill in Manchester, next to a canal that brings coal and cotton and in a city full of workers, but the engine and its coal cost more every year.
look.prompt: Which mill would you build, and what would have to change about coal prices or roads to change your answer?

check.q: What was the main improvement James Watt made to the steam engine?
choices: He made it burn wood instead of coal
He built the first engine that could pump water
He added a separate condenser so the cylinder stayed hot and used far less fuel
He made it small enough to fit in a cottage
check.why: Earlier engines heated and cooled the cylinder every stroke; Watt's condenser cut fuel use to about a quarter.

check.q: How did steam power change where factories could be built?
choices: Factories now had to be near forests
Factories could be built anywhere coal could be delivered, including inside cities
Factories could only be built near coal mines
Factories no longer needed any fuel
check.why: A steam mill did not need a river, so mills moved into cities like Manchester near workers, canals and markets.

check.q: Why did Watt invent the term horsepower?
choices: To measure how fast a train could go
To describe engines used on farms
Because his engines were fueled by hay
To sell engines by comparing their work to the horses they replaced
check.why: Buyers understood horses, so Watt rated his engines by how many horses' work they could do.

lessons.title: Life Inside the Factory
lessons.mainIdea: The factory system replaced the rhythms of home and farm with the clock, the bell and the machine, and made discipline, not skill, the first demand on workers.
reading: A *factory* is a building where many workers use power-driven machines under one owner's control. That definition sounds simple, but it changed daily life more than any invention. On a farm or in a cottage, people worked hard but set their own pace: fast before a harvest, slow on a rainy day, with a break when the baby cried. A machine does not care about rain or babies. It runs at one speed, and the workers must match it. Mill owners posted rules, rang bells and fined workers for lateness, talking, opening a window or leaving a machine unattended.

The clock became a tool of control. Many workers in 1800 did not own a watch, so the factory bell told them the time, and some owners were accused of setting mill clocks forward in the morning and back at night. Work that used to follow the sun now followed the shift. Historians call this the new *discipline* of industrial time, and it is why we still talk about being on the clock. Children were valued in early mills partly because they were small enough to crawl under machines and partly because they could be trained to obey before they learned any other way to work.

Machines also broke skilled trades into simple tasks. A hand weaver knew a whole craft. A power-loom minder watched several machines and tied broken threads. This *division of labor* made goods cheaper and let owners hire people with no training, including women and children, at lower wages. Adam Smith, a Scottish thinker, described in 1776 how splitting pin-making into eighteen separate steps let ten workers make tens of thousands of pins a day instead of a handful each. The gain in output was real. So was the loss of the pride and independence a craft had given.

Wages in the mills were often higher than in farm work, which is why people came. But work was dangerous. Unfenced gears and belts caught hair, hands and clothing. Cotton dust filled lungs. Hours ran twelve to fourteen a day before the Factory Acts, and a worker who was injured or too old was simply let go. Owners argued that they were competing with other mills and could not afford to be generous. Workers argued that the wealth of Manchester was built from their bodies. Both were describing the same system from different ends.

words.d: a building where many workers use power-driven machines under one owner's control
strict rules and control over how and when people work
splitting a job into small separate tasks, each done by a different worker

look.title: The Pin Factory
look.text: Adam Smith described a small pin workshop where the work was split into about eighteen steps: one man draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, and so on. He wrote that ten workers organized this way could make many thousands of pins in a day, while a single worker doing every step alone might struggle to make even twenty.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Smith is explaining why division of labor makes goods cheap. What might a worker who spends every day pointing wire say about the same arrangement?

check.q: How did factory work differ most from cottage or farm work?
choices: Factory work paid nothing
Factory work was done outdoors
Workers had to match the steady pace of machines instead of setting their own
Factories had no rules
check.why: Machines ran at one speed all day, so bells, clocks and fines forced workers to keep up regardless of weather or family.

check.q: Why did early mill owners hire so many children?
choices: Children were small enough for the machines and could be trained to obey, and they were paid less
Laws required mills to employ children
Children were stronger than adults
Adults refused to work in mills
check.why: Children fit under machines, cost less, and had not learned the independent habits of craft workers.

check.q: What did Adam Smith's pin factory example show?
choices: That pins were the most valuable product in Britain
That splitting a job into small steps greatly increased output
That skilled craftsmen made the best pins
That steam engines were needed to make pins
check.why: By dividing pin-making into about eighteen tasks, ten workers made thousands of pins a day instead of a few each.

lessons.title: The Railroad Age
lessons.mainIdea: Railroads shrank distance, created a new market for iron and coal, and set the pace of an economy that now ran on timetables.
reading: On September 15, 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened with a parade of trains, bands and the prime minister on board. It also produced the first famous railway death: a member of Parliament stepped onto the track to greet the prime minister and was hit by a *locomotive*. The engine was Stephenson's Rocket, which had won a contest the year before by running about thirty miles an hour. The railway carried cotton, coal and, to everyone's surprise, huge numbers of passengers. People who had never traveled thirty miles from home could now go to the next city and be back by dinner.

Railways spread with astonishing speed. Britain had about one hundred miles of track in 1830 and about six thousand miles by 1850. Building them took armies of laborers, called navvies, who dug cuttings and tunnels with picks and shovels and moved into the next valley when they finished. Railways were the biggest customers for iron and coal, so they fed the very industries that built them. They also needed money on a scale no single owner had, so investors bought shares in railway companies, and a mania for railway stock in the 1840s made some rich and ruined others.

The railway changed the map of time. Before trains, every town kept its own clock by the sun, so noon in Bristol came about ten minutes after noon in London. Timetables could not work that way. In the 1840s British railways adopted a single time, Greenwich time, and towns followed. The United States divided itself into standard time zones in 1883 for the same reason. Fresh milk and fish reached cities overnight. Newspapers printed in London were read in the north the same day. The *infrastructure*, the basic network a society runs on, had changed, and so had people's sense of how big the world was.

Railroads also reshaped the countryside and the city. Lines cut through farms and old neighborhoods; in London, working-class districts were cleared to build stations, pushing families into more crowded streets nearby. Country markets that the railway skipped withered. Towns at junctions boomed. In Illinois the same story unfolded a generation later: Chicago, with a few thousand people in 1840, became the railway hub of the continent by the 1850s, and grain, lumber and cattle from a thousand miles around flowed through it. A railway map is a map of where the money went.

words.d: a steam-powered engine that pulls a train
the basic networks a society runs on, such as roads, rails, canals, water and power
a published schedule of when trains arrive and leave

look.title: Railway Track in Britain
look.prompt: Which decade saw the fastest growth? What would that decade's demand for iron, coal and labor have looked like?

check.q: Why were railways such important customers for other industries?
choices: They bought most of Britain's cotton cloth
They needed enormous amounts of iron and coal, feeding the industries that built them
They paid farmers to grow food for passengers
They imported all their engines from America
check.why: Rails, locomotives and bridges consumed iron, and engines burned coal, so railways drove the growth of both industries.

check.q: Why did railways lead to a single standard time?
choices: Timetables could not work when every town set its clock by the sun
Parliament wanted everyone to wake up earlier
Trains could not run at night
The Greenwich observatory owned the railways
check.why: With local noon differing by minutes from town to town, schedules were impossible until railways adopted one time.

check.q: What happened to Chicago as railroads spread in the 1850s?
choices: It lost people to towns the railway skipped
It stayed a small farm town
It was cleared to build a single station
It became the rail hub of the continent, and goods from a thousand miles around flowed through it
check.why: Chicago's position at the meeting point of many lines made it the center of the grain, lumber and cattle trade.

lessons.title: The Shock City
lessons.mainIdea: Industrial cities grew faster than anyone could plan for, packing workers into crowded, unsanitary housing where disease killed the young in staggering numbers.
reading: Manchester had about seventy-five thousand people in 1801 and more than three hundred thousand by 1851. No city had ever grown that fast. Visitors came from across Europe to see it, and many were horrified. Streets ran with waste. Families crowded into cellars with no windows and no drains. Rows of back-to-back houses shared a single privy, an outdoor toilet, among dozens of people. Rivers that powered the first mills became open sewers. The German writer Friedrich Engels, whose father owned a Manchester cotton business, walked the worst districts in 1842 and 1843 and wrote a book about what he saw.

Nobody designed this. *Urbanization*, the movement of people into cities, happened because that was where the jobs were, and builders threw up cheap housing as fast as they could. No law required drains or clean water. City governments were weak and often run by the same men who owned the mills. The result was disease. Cholera, spread by water polluted with sewage, killed tens of thousands in Britain in 1832 and again in 1848 and 1849. Typhus and tuberculosis were constant. In the poorest parts of Manchester and Liverpool in the 1840s, a large share of children died before their fifth birthday.

Reformers gathered evidence. Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report on the health of the working population used tables of deaths by district to show that the poor in cities died years earlier than the rich, and that filth, not bad character, was the cause. John Snow, a London doctor, mapped cholera deaths in 1854 around a single water pump and showed the disease came from the water, not from bad air as most people believed. Such reports pushed Parliament toward public health laws in 1848 and 1875 that required sewers, clean water and inspectors.

The industrial city was also a place of energy and hope. It had libraries, newspapers, chapels, music halls, political meetings and the chance to rise. A country girl who came to Manchester to work found wages, friends and a life her mother never had. Immigrants from Ireland, fleeing famine in the late 1840s, filled the poorest streets and kept the mills running. Chicago in the 1880s repeated the pattern with newcomers from Germany, Poland, Italy and the American South, and with the same crowded blocks and the same fights over water and sewers. The shock city was cruel and alive at once.

words.d: the growth of cities as people move into them from the countryside
a deadly disease spread by water polluted with sewage
government action to protect the health of a whole population, such as clean water and sewers

look.title: How Fast Manchester Grew
look.prompt: If a city quadruples in fifty years, what has to be built to keep up? What happens if it is not built?

check.q: Why did cholera spread so easily in industrial cities?
choices: Factories released it in their smoke
Drinking water was polluted with sewage because there were no drains or clean supplies
It came from cotton dust
Trains carried it from the countryside
check.why: Cholera lives in water fouled by human waste, and crowded districts without sewers or clean water spread it quickly.

check.q: What did Chadwick's 1842 report use to make its case?
choices: Tables of deaths by district showing the poor died earlier because of filth
Interviews with mill owners about profits
Maps of railway lines
Sermons about the character of the poor
check.why: Chadwick used death statistics to show that living conditions, not personal failings, cut short the lives of the urban poor.

check.q: Which statement about the industrial city is best supported by the lesson?
choices: It was uniformly hopeless for everyone who lived there
Its problems were quickly solved by mill owners
It was both deadly and full of opportunity, and reforms came only after evidence was gathered
It grew slowly under careful planning
check.why: The city killed the poor through disease yet offered wages and freedom, and public health laws followed reports like Chadwick's and Snow's.

lessons.title: Children, Inspectors and the Law
lessons.mainIdea: Investigations into child labor produced the first factory laws, which were weak at first but established that government could regulate work.
reading: For decades mill owners and many members of Parliament argued that the government had no business inside a factory. A contract between an owner and a worker, they said, was private. If a parent chose to send a child to a mill, that was the family's affair. Besides, Britain competed with other countries, and shorter hours would mean higher prices and lost sales. These arguments came from a belief called *laissez-faire*, a French phrase meaning leave it alone: the economy works best when the government keeps out.

What changed minds was evidence. In 1832 a committee led by Michael Sadler took testimony from workers who had grown up in the mills. Witnesses described starting work at six years old, shifts of fourteen hours or more during busy seasons, beatings to keep them awake, and bodies bent from years of standing. Some could not stand straight when they testified. Newspapers printed the testimony. Owners complained that the witnesses were picked to shock, and a second inquiry the next year gave a more careful picture, but it agreed that children were being worked far beyond what their bodies could bear.

The Factory Act of 1833 was the result. It banned children under nine from textile mills, limited those under thirteen to nine hours a day, and for the first time paid inspectors to check. Four inspectors for the whole country could not visit every mill, and owners lied about ages and hid children when the inspector came. But the principle was set. In 1842 a Mines Act barred women and children under ten from working underground after a report with pictures of children hauling coal carts on hands and knees. In 1847 a Ten Hours Act limited women and young people in textile mills to ten hours a day, which in practice shortened men's hours too.

Illinois followed the same path decades later. In 1893 the state passed a law limiting factory work for children and hired Florence Kelley, who lived at Hull House in Chicago, as its first chief factory inspector. Her team walked into sweatshops and documented children as young as four sewing garments. The Illinois Supreme Court struck down part of the law two years later, and the fight continued for a generation. The pattern was the same as in Britain: private suffering became public evidence, evidence became law, and law was then tested, resisted and slowly enforced.

words.d: the belief that government should leave the economy alone and not regulate business
an official whose job is to visit workplaces and check that laws are obeyed
a statement given as evidence, often before a court or committee

look.title: Before the Committee
look.text: Witnesses before the 1832 committee described beginning mill work as young as six, working from five or six in the morning until eight or nine at night during busy seasons, and being struck with a strap by the overlooker when they slowed or fell asleep. Several said their limbs had become bent from years of standing at the machines and that they had had no time for school.
look.cite: Testimony to the Sadler Committee, British Parliament, 1832 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Owners said these witnesses were chosen to shock Parliament. Does that make the testimony useless as evidence? What else would you want to see?

check.q: What did believers in laissez-faire argue about factory laws?
choices: That the government should set all wages
That inspectors should live in the mills
That children should own the factories
That work was a private contract and government should keep out of it
check.why: Laissez-faire held that the economy worked best when government left agreements between owners and workers alone.

check.q: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do that earlier laws had not?
choices: It paid inspectors to enforce the rules
It banned all child labor in Britain
It closed the textile mills
It gave workers the right to vote
check.why: Earlier laws had no enforcement; the 1833 act hired four inspectors, which made the rules real for the first time.

check.q: Who was Florence Kelley?
choices: A Manchester mill owner
A witness before the Sadler Committee
Illinois's first chief factory inspector, who documented child labor in Chicago sweatshops
The author of the Mines Act
check.why: Kelley, based at Hull House, enforced the 1893 Illinois child labor law until the state supreme court weakened it.

lessons.title: Unions and the Strike
lessons.mainIdea: Workers learned that acting together gave them power an individual lacked, and they built unions, strikes and political movements despite laws against them.
reading: A single worker who asked for higher pay could be fired and replaced by the next person at the gate. A thousand workers who stopped at once could stop the mill. This simple arithmetic is the idea behind a *union*, an organization of workers who bargain with an employer together. Britain outlawed unions in 1799 and 1800, fearing revolution like France's, and workers met in secret. Parliament lifted the ban in 1824, though for decades the courts still punished strikes in various ways. Skilled workers such as engineers and printers organized first, since they were hardest to replace.

A *strike*, when workers refuse to work until a demand is met, was the union's main weapon and a risky one. Strikers earned nothing, and owners could bring in replacements or simply wait. In 1834 six farm laborers in the village of Tolpuddle were sentenced to seven years' transportation to Australia for swearing a secret oath to form a union. Hundreds of thousands of people signed petitions and marched in London, and the government gave in and pardoned them. The Tolpuddle Martyrs, as they were called, showed that public opinion could shift.

Workers also turned to politics. In 1838 a movement called Chartism demanded the vote for every adult man, secret ballots, and pay for members of Parliament so that working men could serve. Chartists gathered millions of signatures on petitions in 1839, 1842 and 1848. Parliament rejected all three. Yet within seventy years every one of the Charter's main demands had become law. In the United States, workers marched in Chicago on May 1, 1886, for an eight-hour day. Days later a bomb at a rally in Haymarket Square killed police and civilians, and the trial and executions that followed became a symbol for workers around the world. May Day, the international workers' holiday, comes from Chicago.

Unions did not win everything, and they often excluded women, immigrants and Black workers from their ranks. Owners fought them with lockouts, blacklists and private guards. But over the 1800s wages in Britain rose, hours fell, and a worker's voice in the workplace became normal in a way it had not been in 1800. Economists still debate how much of that came from unions and how much from growth itself. What is not in doubt is that workers who could not vote, and who were told the economy was none of their business, made it their business anyway.

words.d: an organization of workers who bargain with an employer as a group
when workers refuse to work until a demand is met
a British working-class movement of the 1830s and 1840s demanding the vote for all men

look.title: Alone or Together
look.text: Forty spinners in one mill room each earn the same wage. One asks the owner for a raise and is fired that afternoon; there are a dozen people waiting for the job. The next month all forty agree to stop at the same hour and stay out until the owner talks to them. They have no savings, and their rent is due Friday.
look.prompt: What can the forty do that the one could not? What could still make them lose, and how might they prepare for it?

check.q: Why does a union give workers power that one worker lacks?
choices: Because unions can fire the owner
Because one worker can be replaced but a whole workforce stopping at once can shut down the mill
Because unions were always legal
Because union members were paid by the government
check.why: The owner can replace one person easily, but not everyone at once, so collective action changes the balance.

check.q: What did the case of the Tolpuddle Martyrs show?
choices: That strikes always succeeded
That Parliament supported unions from the start
That Australia welcomed British workers
That public protest could force the government to back down
check.why: Massive petitions and marches led the government to pardon six farm workers sent to Australia for forming a union.

check.q: What happened to the Chartists' demands in the long run?
choices: Every main demand eventually became law, though Parliament rejected the petitions at the time
They were adopted immediately in 1839
They were never adopted in Britain
They were adopted only in the United States
check.why: Parliament rejected the petitions, but within seventy years the vote for men, secret ballots and paid members were all law.

lessons.title: Marx and the Critics of Capitalism
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers from Adam Smith to Karl Marx argued about whether the new economy was fair and whether it should be left alone, reformed or overthrown.
reading: The Industrial Revolution created a new kind of economy that people began calling *capitalism*: private owners put up capital, hire workers for wages, and sell goods for profit in competitive markets. Adam Smith had argued in 1776 that when each person pursues his own gain, competition tends to produce more goods at lower prices, as if guided by an invisible hand. Smith also warned that owners would try to fix prices and that repetitive work dulled the mind. Later thinkers who took his name, though, often kept only the first idea.

Others looked at Manchester and saw not an invisible hand but a fist. Robert Owen, a mill owner in Scotland, shortened hours, built schools and decent housing at his mill in New Lanark, and made a profit doing it. He argued that owners could be humane. Reformers in Parliament pushed factory and health laws. And Friedrich Engels, after his walks through Manchester, teamed up with a German philosopher named Karl Marx. In 1848 they published a short pamphlet, the Communist Manifesto, in London.

Marx argued that history was a struggle between classes. In the industrial age the two great classes were the *bourgeoisie*, the owners of factories and capital, and the *proletariat*, the workers who owned nothing but their ability to work. Owners grew rich, he said, from the difference between what workers produced and what they were paid. Competition would push wages down and concentrate wealth until workers, who were the great majority, rose up, took the factories and ran them in common. The Manifesto ended by telling the workers of all countries to unite; they had nothing to lose but their chains.

Marx's predictions did not come true in the way he expected. Wages in industrial countries rose over the long run, and the revolutions that later claimed his name took place in poor farming countries, not in Britain. Critics said he ignored how markets and reforms could improve life without revolution. But his questions did not go away: who owns what, who gets the gain from new machines, and whether workers have a say. Every debate today about automation, wages and inequality is, in part, a debate that Smith, Owen and Marx started.

words.d: an economy in which private owners invest money, hire workers for wages and sell goods for profit
Marx's word for the class that owns factories and capital
Marx's word for the class of workers who own nothing but their ability to work

look.title: Nothing to Lose but Their Chains
look.text: Marx and Engels wrote that the history of all societies so far had been a history of class struggles. In the modern age, they argued, that struggle had simplified into two camps facing each other: the bourgeoisie, who owned capital, and the proletariat, who had only their labor to sell. They closed by declaring that workers had nothing to lose but their chains and had a world to win, and they called on the workers of all countries to unite.
look.cite: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Communist Manifesto, 1848 (translated and paraphrased)
look.prompt: Marx wrote this in the year of the 1848 revolutions and just after Engels's walks through Manchester. What evidence from this chapter would support his view? What evidence would challenge it?

check.q: Which of these is a feature of capitalism as the lesson defines it?
choices: Private owners invest capital, hire workers for wages and sell goods for profit
The government owns all factories
Workers own the factories in common
Goods are traded without money
check.why: Capitalism rests on private ownership, wage labor and competitive markets.

check.q: How did Robert Owen differ from Marx?
choices: Owen called for revolution while Marx called for reform
Owen believed owners could treat workers well and still profit, while Marx expected class conflict to end the system
Owen was a worker and Marx was a mill owner
Owen opposed all factory laws
check.why: Owen ran a humane mill at New Lanark to prove reform worked; Marx argued the system itself would drive workers to overthrow it.

check.q: Which of Marx's predictions did not come true as he expected?
choices: That factories would use machines
That cities would keep growing
That there would be owners and workers
That wages in industrial countries would keep falling until workers rose up
check.why: Wages in industrial nations rose over the long run, and revolutions in his name happened in farming countries instead.

lessons.title: Europe, America and Japan Catch Up
lessons.mainIdea: Industry spread beyond Britain when other nations copied its machines and added their own resources, banks and government support.
reading: Britain tried to keep its lead. For years it was illegal to export textile machinery or for skilled mechanics to leave the country. It did not work. Samuel Slater memorized the design of Arkwright's machines, sailed to America in 1789, and built a cotton mill in Rhode Island. Belgium, with coal and iron near French and Dutch markets, industrialized in the 1820s and 1830s. France grew more slowly, keeping many small workshops. The German states, once they linked their markets and built railways in the 1840s and 1850s, moved fast, and by 1900 Germany led Europe in steel and chemicals.

The United States had what Britain lacked: endless land, rivers for power, and immigrants for labor. Mills at Lowell, Massachusetts, in the 1820s hired young farm women and housed them in supervised boardinghouses. After the Civil War the country built railroads across a continent and drew iron ore, coal and oil from the interior. By the 1890s the United States made more steel than Britain. The Midwest became the workshop of the country. In Chicago, Cyrus McCormick built a factory in 1847 to make reaping machines that cut wheat, and by the 1880s the city's stockyards turned cattle into packaged meat on moving *assembly lines* that would inspire Henry Ford.

Japan is the most remarkable case, because it industrialized on purpose. After American warships forced Japan to open its ports in the 1850s, a new government under the Meiji emperor decided in 1868 that the only way to avoid being colonized was to become as strong as the colonizers. It sent students and officials abroad to study factories, banks and armies. It built the first railway in 1872, opened a model silk mill the same year with French machines and French instructors, and then sold state factories to private companies. Within forty years Japan had a modern army and navy and a growing textile industry, and in 1905 it defeated Russia in war.

Two lessons stand out. First, later industrializers did not have to invent; they copied, and they could skip Britain's slow early steps. Second, governments mattered more the later a country started. Britain's revolution grew from private business with little state help. Germany's used banks and tariffs, taxes on imports that protected new factories. Japan's was planned from the top. The spread of industry was not automatic. It went where resources, capital and political will came together, and it left much of the world, including the colonies that supplied cotton and other raw materials, on the outside.

words.d: a tax on imported goods, often used to protect a country's own industries
a way of making things in which the product moves past workers who each do one task
the era of the Japanese emperor who reigned from 1868, when Japan modernized rapidly

look.title: The Mission Abroad
look.text: In 1871 a group of Japanese officials sets out on a two-year journey to the United States and Europe. They tour shipyards in Britain, steel works in Germany, schools in France and factories in Chicago. They take notes on everything: how taxes are collected, how officers are trained, how a bank issues paper money. When they return, they must decide what to copy and what to leave alone.
look.prompt: Why might a country choose to copy another's factories but not its form of government? What are the risks of copying too much or too little?

check.q: How did Samuel Slater bring the Industrial Revolution to America?
choices: He bought machines legally from Britain
He invented the water frame himself
He memorized British machine designs, left secretly, and built a mill in Rhode Island
He was sent by the British government
check.why: Britain banned exporting machines and mechanics, so Slater carried the designs in his head and rebuilt them in America.

check.q: Why did Japan's government decide to industrialize after 1868?
choices: To avoid being colonized by becoming as strong as Western powers
Because Britain ordered it to
To sell silk to China
Because its emperor wanted to move to Europe
check.why: Having been forced open by American warships, Japan's leaders concluded that only modern industry and armies could keep it independent.

check.q: What difference did starting later make for countries like Germany and Japan?
choices: They had to invent every machine again
They needed no coal or iron
They industrialized more slowly than Britain
They could copy proven methods, and their governments played a bigger role
check.why: Later industrializers borrowed British technology and used banks, tariffs or state planning to catch up quickly.

lessons.title: Steel, Wires and Light
lessons.mainIdea: A second wave of technology after 1850, built on steel, electricity and the telegraph, made industry faster, bigger and more connected than the age of steam.
reading: The first Industrial Revolution ran on iron, coal and steam. The second, starting around 1850, ran on *steel*, electricity, chemicals and oil. Steel is iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon; it is stronger and more flexible than iron but had always been slow and expensive to make. In 1856 Henry Bessemer in England announced a process that blew air through molten iron to burn out impurities, turning tons of iron into steel in minutes. Prices fell sharply. Steel rails lasted many times longer than iron ones. Steel beams let architects in Chicago build the first skyscrapers in the 1880s.

Electricity changed communication first. In 1844 Samuel Morse sent a message by *telegraph* from Washington to Baltimore over a wire, using a code of dots and dashes. Within a decade wires ran beside every railway. In 1866 a cable across the Atlantic seabed linked Britain and North America, and a message that had taken ten days by ship took minutes. Prices, news and orders now moved faster than any goods, and a merchant in Chicago could know the price of wheat in Liverpool the same morning. The telephone followed in 1876.

Then electricity became power and light. In 1879 Thomas Edison's team produced a practical light bulb, and in 1882 his company opened a generating station in New York that lit a few blocks of offices. Electric streetcars appeared in the late 1880s and let cities spread outward. Electric motors could be put anywhere a wire reached, so a factory no longer needed a single giant steam engine with belts running to every machine. By 1900 the second revolution had also given the world cheap chemical dyes, the internal combustion engine, and the first automobiles.

This wave belonged as much to Germany and the United States as to Britain. It depended on science in a new way. Bessemer was a tinkerer, but the chemists who built Germany's dye industry had university degrees, and companies began to run research laboratories. The scale of business grew too. Steel mills and electric companies needed millions in capital, so *corporations* selling shares to thousands of investors replaced family firms. Andrew Carnegie's steel company and Standard Oil were larger than many governments. The question of who would check that kind of power was new.

words.d: iron mixed with a small, controlled amount of carbon, making it stronger and more flexible
a system for sending coded messages instantly over electric wires
a business owned by many investors who buy shares in it

look.title: Ten Days to Ten Minutes
look.text: In 1865 a cotton merchant in Liverpool wants to know the price of cotton in New York. He must wait for a ship, about ten days each way. In 1867 the same merchant walks to the telegraph office and has an answer before lunch. His rival across the street can do the same.
look.prompt: How does the telegraph change the merchant's decisions about buying and selling? Who gains and who loses when everyone knows prices at the same time?

check.q: Why did the Bessemer process matter?
choices: It made steel cheap and fast to produce, allowing longer-lasting rails and tall buildings
It was the first way to make iron
It replaced coal with electricity in furnaces
It let factories run without workers
check.why: Blowing air through molten iron turned it to steel in minutes, dropping prices and opening the way for steel rails and skyscrapers.

check.q: What did the 1866 transatlantic cable change?
choices: Ships could cross the Atlantic in a day
Messages between Britain and North America went from days to minutes
Cotton could be shipped by wire
Britain and America became one country
check.why: The undersea telegraph cable let news and prices cross the ocean almost instantly instead of by ten-day ship voyage.

check.q: How did the second industrial revolution differ from the first?
choices: It used no machines
It happened only in Britain
It depended more on science, research labs and huge corporations
It relied entirely on water power
check.why: Chemicals and electricity required trained scientists, and steel and electric companies needed capital from thousands of investors.

lessons.title: New Air, New Time, New Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Industrialization remade the environment and daily life, bringing cheaper goods, longer lives and new freedoms alongside smoke, pollution and a faster world.
reading: Stand on a hill above an industrial city in 1880 and you would not see it. Smoke from thousands of chimneys hung over Manchester, Pittsburgh and Chicago so thick that trees died and white shirts turned gray by noon. Rivers ran orange with dye or black with oil. Coal ash coated everything. In 1900 people accepted this as the price of jobs; a smoking chimney meant a working mill. Only much later would scientists link that smoke to disease and to the warming of the planet. The Industrial Revolution began humanity's large-scale burning of *fossil fuels*, and the air has carried the record ever since.

The land changed too. Forests fell for railway ties and mine timbers. Wheat from Illinois and Argentina, moved by rail and steamship, fed European cities and pushed local farmers off the land. Whole regions were dug up for coal and ore. Yet the same forces made goods cheap. In 1800 a working family in England owned a few garments and mended them for years. By 1900 that family could buy machine-made cotton clothes, factory shoes, tinned food, cheap newspapers and a railway ticket to the seaside. *Consumption*, the buying and using of goods, became part of ordinary life.

Time itself felt different. The clock ruled work, and it now ruled leisure: the Saturday half-day, the annual holiday, the timetable. Gas and then electric light stretched the day into the night. Literacy rose as governments built schools, partly to produce workers who could read instructions. Women's lives shifted in contradictory ways. Factory wages gave some young women independence their mothers never had, while middle-class women were increasingly expected to stay home. Families grew smaller as children became a cost rather than a set of hands.

Was it worth it? People in 1900 lived longer on average than in 1800, in Britain by more than a decade, largely because of clean water, cheaper food and later medicine. They also worked to a bell, breathed smoke and lived in cities where a lost job meant hunger. The gains and losses did not fall on the same people. A mill owner's grandson and a mill child's grandson experienced different revolutions. Any honest judgment has to hold both in view, and to notice that many of the questions, about pollution, machines and who benefits, are still open.

words.d: coal, oil or natural gas, formed from ancient living things and burned for energy
buying and using goods and services
the ability to read and write

look.title: Two Grandsons
look.text: In 1900 two old men sit in the same Manchester park. One is the grandson of a mill owner; he went to university, owns shares in a steel company, and takes the train to the coast each August. The other is the grandson of a mill child; he can read, earns steady wages, and lives in a brick house with a tap, but his lungs are weak and he has never been more than twenty miles from the city.
look.prompt: Compare each man's life to what his grandfather had in 1800. Who gained more? Is that the right question?

check.q: What long-term environmental change did the Industrial Revolution begin?
choices: The end of coal mining
The clearing of all cities
The cooling of the planet
Large-scale burning of fossil fuels, filling the air with smoke and carbon
check.why: Coal-fired industry started humanity's massive use of fossil fuels, with effects on air and climate that continue today.

check.q: How did cheap machine-made goods change ordinary families by 1900?
choices: Families could buy clothes, shoes, tinned food and newspapers they could not afford in 1800
Families stopped needing money
Families made all their own goods at home
Families owned fewer things than in 1800
check.why: Mass production made everyday goods affordable, and buying things became part of working-class life.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the gains and losses did not fall on the same people?
choices: Because everyone benefited equally
Because owners and workers experienced very different versions of the same revolution
Because only farmers gained
Because no one lived longer in 1900
check.why: Life expectancy rose overall, but an owner's family and a worker's family shared neither the wealth nor the smoke equally.

review.q: Which combination best explains why Britain industrialized first?
choices: Cheap coal, available capital, canals and laws protecting property
A large population and a strong king
Its colonies in Africa
Its warm climate
review.why: Coal, capital, transport and stable laws came together in Britain around 1750 in a way they did nowhere else.

review.q: Why did Arkwright's water frame move cloth-making out of the home?
choices: Homes were banned from making cloth
The machine needed a river for power and was too large for a cottage
Cotton could not be spun by hand
Merchants refused to buy home-made cloth
review.why: Water power required a mill by a river, so workers came to the machines, creating the factory.

review.q: What did James Watt's separate condenser accomplish?
choices: It made engines run on wood
It made engines move trains
It cut the fuel a steam engine used to about a quarter
It invented the horse
review.why: Keeping the cylinder hot saved most of the fuel, making steam practical for mills.

review.q: Why did railways lead to standard time?
choices: Passengers demanded it
Every town's sun time made timetables impossible
Trains ran only at noon
Parliament wanted one clock for taxes
review.why: Timetables need one clock, so British railways adopted Greenwich time and towns followed.

review.q: What was the main cause of cholera in industrial cities?
choices: Cotton dust in the air
Long working hours
Cold weather
Drinking water polluted with sewage
review.why: John Snow's 1854 pump map and later science showed cholera spread through fouled water.

review.q: What principle did the Factory Act of 1833 establish?
choices: That government could regulate work and enforce it with inspectors
That children could not work anywhere
That mills must be owned by the state
That unions were legal
review.why: The act was weak, but paid inspectors meant the government had claimed the right to look inside the factory.

review.q: According to Marx, where did the owners' profit come from?
choices: Government subsidies
Selling goods abroad
The difference between what workers produced and what they were paid
The invisible hand of the market
review.why: Marx argued that the bourgeoisie grew rich by keeping the value workers created beyond their wages.

choices: It happened by accident through private business
It was forced on Japan by British occupation
It never happened
It was planned by the government to keep Japan independent
review.why: The Meiji government studied Western industry abroad and built railways, mills and a modern army on purpose.
